utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Carrier, before we continue, I would like to -- I'd like to briefly raise today and tomorrow as far as scheduling is concerned. First of all, the Chamber, looking at the improvement of avoiding repetition, et cetera, which you showed et cetera, the Chamber is quite confident that you would be able, with similar improvement, be able to finish in approximately 40, 45 minutes today. Then, could I ask the other parties how much time they would need for re-examination? Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, as things stand now, I would use half a session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Half a session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So let's then try to see whether we could conclude the testimony of this witness at the end of the first session. Mr. Mikulicic, for the next witness how much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The next witness will be Mr. Kuzmanovic, and he needs two sessions at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two sessions --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Two to three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two to three.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I hear from the other parties for Witness MM-5 is the next ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At this point, Mr. President, on behalf of the Gotovina Defence, I would anticipate half an hour to 45 minutes at most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I can see nothing arising for my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which -- Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think we had two sessions, and based on the witness statement, that's certainly enough. But I don't know what the oral examination will reveal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which means that there's a reasonable expectation that we could finish the next witness by tomorrow, the end of the morning. I urge the parties all to strictly adhere to the estimates, of course, to the extent possible, but to try to do our utmost best. Mr. Carrier, then -- I'll first, Mr. Pejkovic, sorry for discussing matters which have only partly to do with you. Mr. Pejkovic, I would like to remind you that the solemn declaration that you gave at the beginning of your testimony that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth is still binding. Mr. Carrier will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, could we have Exhibit D428 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, what is coming up on the screen is what we were looking at yesterday, the Programme for Return.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if you could turn to page 8 in the English, 5 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Pejkovic, looking at number 13 enumerated in this programme, it starts at the bottom of the page in English and goes on to the next page where it says that: "All categories of persons defined under the Geneva Conventions from 1951 as stated in paragraph 1 of the basic principles of this programme who do not have Croatian documents may return after special approval by the office for expelled persons and refugees and following checks made by the Ministry of the Interior." And then it goes on. Yesterday, you did talk a little bit about some of the Croatian document issues. This -- number 13 in this list, this indicates that all refugees now can -- that don't have Croatian documents, there's a new process - isn't that right - for obtaining those documents?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 13 of the return programme defines the category of all those people who are considered refugees who can return following a special approval of the office if they do not have Croatian documents. Once back, they can regulate their status with the Ministry of the Interior, they can obtain residence and be issued with IDs. And if they apply for them, they will receive their passports as well. Mention is made of the Ministry of the Interior because once a return application is submitted, the Ministry of the Interior ran checks on the citizenship of the person involved. If the person is found to be a Croatian citizen, such a person would receive a certificate of the return programme with which it could return to the Republic of Croatia. Such a person could also go to the nearest Croatian mission to be issued with a travel document which in turn could be used for the person's return to the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, the -- before this programme which was instituted in 1998, the Serbs that had fled didn't have any Croatian documents before they fled Croatia, they found it very difficult to obtain these documents and return to Croatia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not. They could rely on the consular services of the various Croatian missions abroad and ask for travel documents which would enable them to return to the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we please have 65 ter 847 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, I want to review a few documents with you and then ask you some questions. The document that's coming up on the screen is a report on the situation of human rights in Croatia. It's to the commission on human rights. It's dated 31 October 1997 from the UN Special Rapporteur Elisabeth Rehn.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And if we could, please, turn to paragraph 52, which is -- should be page 13 in the English, 14 and 15 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And I'll just read this to you, Mr. Pejkovic. Paragraph 52 says: "The special rapporteur is concerned about restrictive conditions imposed on return to the country by Croatian Serb refugees in possession of valid citizenship certificates. The" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel, could we just put that on the screen, please, paragraph 52.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: "The domovnica refugees who" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you are reading from paragraph 52, then perhaps the previous page would serve us better, in English. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: "Refugees who intend to" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I still have 53 on my -- you are quoting from 52, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we're waiting for this to come up, this document is Exhibit D684 that's in evidence already. That would be 65 ter 847.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Continuing: "Refugees who intend to repatriate, whether with the help of the UNHCR or spontaneously on the basis of the domovnica are no longer able to cross the border without first obtaining additional travel documents from a Croatian embassy abroad. However, there is no established procedure for Croatian citizens to obtain valid passports or travel documents from Croatian embassies in neighbouring countries. In addition, Croatian embassies do not accept applications for a domovnica" -- and if we turn over into paragraph 53, there's a further discussion about a special category of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And if we could now have document 65 ter 7503 on the screen, please. And, Mr. President, I'm informed that D684 does not have a B/C/S translation, so if the translation for the 65 ter number I just referred to could be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a look at it, and then the question is whether we need a new exhibit number or whether the B/C/S translation should be uploaded. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, this is a document, 31st March, 1998. It's a Reuters report entitled "Zagreb's New Refugees ... Plan Lacks Details." I just want to go through the first six paragraphs with you. It says: "The Croatian government said on Tuesday it was cutting some of the red tape preventing the return of Serb refugees, but a comprehensive plan - demanded by the West - would not be complete before mid-June. "The government adopted a document specifying a new legal procedure for the individual return of all refugees including Serbs, government spokesman Neven Jurica told a news conference." And then you're quoted here, Mr. Pejkovic: "'The aim of this document is to express our will to allow the return of all of those who wish to do so,' said Lovre Pejkovic, head of the Croatian office for refugees and displaced persons." And then the report goes on: "The main novelty in the nine-point document is that those who fled the country during the 1991-1995 war and now want to come back can apply for the necessary papers in Croatia's representative offices abroad." Next paragraph: "Until now, Serb refugees sheltering in Yugoslavia and the Serb-controlled Bosnia had to find their way around a 'catch-22' situation, where they could not enter Croatia without identity documents which could only be obtained in Croatia." And it says -- there's a quote: "'This is a major step forward,' this is said by Zeljko Trkanjac, spokesman for the foreign ministry, which drafted the document." And, for the benefit of my friends, Exhibit P2594 has similar information and Mr. Pejkovic talking about this new programme in 1998. Mr. Pejkovic, my question for you is: Given these documents and this report, is it not the case that in 1998 the situation changed and there is a new procedure for people outside of Croatia that made it easier for them to get citizenship documents in Croatian, official documents, in order to re-enter the country?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The return programme that you are referring to that was adopted in 1998, and as you referred to it in the documents shown, was a mere continuation of all the processes which had begun earlier on the basis of the documents which had been accepted pursuant to the agreement on the normalisation of relations between the FRY and Croatia, as well as by the signing of the protocol on organised return concluded between the Republic of Croatia and the FRY, as well as the opening of Croatian -- of a Croatian mission and consulate in the territory of the former FRY. As of the moment they were set up, the Serb refugees from Croatia could ask for travel documents so as to be able to return to the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just try to find out whether there's a confusion between the one who puts the questions and the one who answers the questions. I got the impression that Mr. Carrier wants to compare the situation which existed -- well, let's say in the first two years approximately, and then there was an agreement, and then this resulted in a plan which was then in 1998 completed and -- now, I understand from your answer you said: Well, everything that happened as a result of the agreement, so you apparently are talking about 1997 and onwards, where in 1998 some new matters were implemented. Whereas I understand that Mr. Carrier wants to understand what the step forward is in relation to what happened until this agreement, end of 1995, 1996, part of 1997. So let's try to talk about the same thing. Did I understand you well, Mr. Carrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did I understand your answer well? You said: "A mere continuation of all the processes which had begun earlier on the basis of the documents which had been accepted pursuant to the agreement on the normalisation ..." That's 1997, isn't it? So you're talking from 1997 onwards and Mr. Carrier is talking about 1995, 1997, 1998. So it doesn't make -- you're talking about different things. Could you tell us whether this was a major step forward in relation to the time-period Mr. Carrier was referring to, that is, before the time this agreement had been established, that it was difficult then to get your papers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you basically said what I wanted to say, although I may not have been as precise. I wanted to say that the process was initiated in late 1995. It picked up speed once the normalisation of relations agreement was signed, and legally speaking, it was complete with this new refugee return programme of 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, let's get back to -- on from 1995, was it experienced as difficult to get the papers up to the moment where this agreement and the implementation of the agreement in 1997/1998 took place? During these first two years was it considered to be difficult, because that's what most of these reports are talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the FRY between 1995 and the opening of our consulate, one could not be issued with any documents because there was no body which could issue them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it was difficult at that time? Yes. Well, that's what Mr. Carrier apparently wanted to ask you. If you say, We've taken away some of the red - what was it? - the red tape, et cetera, that means there was quite a difference in the situation where it was impossible as reported to obtain the documents at an earlier stage. That was the catch-22 situation which was described. So do I understand that this was the case until the Croatian mission in Belgrade was opened, your consulate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would make an effort to try to understand what Mr. Carrier is exactly asking you and then we get quicker to what appears to be the answer to the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could have that 65 ter document tendered, the Reuters article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit P2677.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2677 is admitted into evidence. The translation of the earlier report - what was it? - it was a D document, if that could be uploaded, it's now available. So if the party that tendered - what was it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 684 which is in e-court without translation, whether that could be uploaded. And I take it that you'll make the translation available so you can get it from the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we'll get it from e-court. We'll have our court officer take a look at that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, could we please have 65 ter 5003 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, in paragraph 5 of your statement, you mentioned after the occupied Croatian territory was liberated during Operations Flash and Storm, many of the people that had been accommodated in the free parts of Croatia had to return to their pre-war places of residence, which entailed, you say, enormous organisational and financial effort. Mr. Pejkovic, the vast majority of the people that you're referring to here are Croats that had been accommodated in the free parts of Croatia before the territory was liberated, you put a number on it around 93 per cent during your testimony. Is that right? That it was the Croats that were returning into the occupied -- or formally occupied territories?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Pejkovic, the Croats that were moving into the newly liberated areas were not necessarily returning to their pre-war residences. Some of the people moving into these areas also included Croats that had taken refuge in the free parts of Croatia, fleeing such places as Bosnia, et cetera. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And during your testimony you mentioned that Croatia was under pressure from these displaced Croats, and you mentioned the associations that were formed to return, the pressures because of the people being accommodated in hotels, the associated costs, et cetera. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, on Monday you were shown a draft decree on the return of expelled persons and refugees to the liberated areas which was an item on the agenda of the 277th Closed Session of government on October 5th, 1995. Do you recall that? You can see it on the screen, the first page.

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time that I see this document, but I do remember the decree on the return of persons that was adopted by the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Well, during your testimony on Monday you were shown D214, I believe, and that's this -- the beginning of this document, including this page, and the decree is attached. But we'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: If you perhaps just scroll through, Mr. Registrar, to page 5 in the English. I'm not sure what the B/C/S is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: It's coming up now, Mr. Pejkovic, but just so that you recognise that. That's the decree you were looking at the other day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, this is Exhibit D214.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes -- well, the witness just told us that, "This is the first time that I see this document," whereas on Monday he testified that he's familiar with the document so --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm just talking about this for the record. It was identified as 65 ter 5003, and I'm just -- I'm clarifying it for the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I thought that D --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: If I could help --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Q. Well, during your testimony on Monday you were shown D214. I believe that's this, the beginning of this document ..." So D214 was referred to by Mr. Carrier. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. And just -- I'm sure it will become apparent in a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, if we could actually turn to --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Registrar, if you could turn to page 4 in the English and page 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, looking at the minutes of this 277th Closed Session, your name's not on the people that attended, the list. Am I correct in assuming that you were not present at this closed session?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't. I wasn't at the meeting, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And did you know that during this closed session that this draft decree, which you talked about before, was discussed by senior members of the Croatian government, including Vice Prime Minister Radic, who was the minister of development and reconstruction?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I never had access to documents -- government documents which were marked as strictly confidential or secret. I was the representative of the office and I read regulations and decrees in the Official Gazette, and as such, that was when they were -- became official, when they were published in the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The answer is simply: No, you were not aware. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And I take it from your last answer that not only were you not given access to confidential documents or secret documents, is it fair to -- is it fair to --

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have access to them, no, to no secret documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first wait what the question will be. Is it fair to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that you weren't included in things like closed sessions of government and private meetings with President Tudjman or anything like that either, to discuss policy or anything like that in terms of passing laws, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't included, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And during your testimony you explained that this decree cancelled the status of certain displaced persons' status; however, did you know that this decree was also discussed and viewed as a means of encouraging Croats, both from Croatia and abroad, to colonise the previous occupied territories?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is the contents of the decree. Now, what you're saying now, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please turn to page 11 in the English and 9 in the B/C/S. And perhaps if we could just turn back one page in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, you can see that these are minutes of a discussion about this decree that was held that day, and item 1 on the agenda is this decree and Mr. Radic is invited by the prime minister to present the chronology and the dilemmas regarding the subject as well as to propose the conclusions on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And if we could please turn the page in the B/C/S, please, and scroll down -- or on to the next page as well, actually, in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, I just want to review a few of the parts of this discussion where your boss, Minister Radic, is talking. And in the English part way down the page - and it's at the very bottom of the B/C/S and it turns on to the next page after that - Mr. Radic says: "... and on the other hand, since it is in our best national interest that these people return to their homes, in our primary national interest, not only that they go back but also that we colonise the vacated Croatian" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may turn the floor to Mr. Misetic on the translation here, and if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would object on the basis of the translation of the word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see what word is bothering you and let's see what ... Could we invite the witness to read or you to read the original of the line where apparently you have some problem with the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's a long sentence, Mr. President, so I'll just read the relevant clause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The great national interest and not only the return, but also the settlement of void Croatian areas or empty Croatian areas." [In English] That's it, that's how I would have translated it myself, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, could you invite the witness to answer any question you may put to him in relation to this text on the basis of his understanding of the Croatian original.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Just to be clear, Mr. Pejkovic, you'll have to do a little work and read along so that you can base your answers on what you're reading and I'll continue with what it says here. "We ought to define a number of stimulating measures" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, if you could just follow what Mr. Carrier reads to you in your own language. So of course it will be translated to you, but at the same time you'll be able to see on the screen what the text of the transcript exactly is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could just check, because what I'm looking at in e-court is not the page in B/C/S, so I'm not sure that the right page in B/C/S is there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we first have to find the right page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's the one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and that starts, I think, in the top: "Veliki nacionalni interes" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it will be much easier to provide the witness with a hard copy of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if there is one, it's fine. If not, then we'll do with -- is -- if anyone has a hard copy, but we're not going to produce it now. And that will take at least a couple of minutes. Mr. Carrier, if you can -- that's great -- Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I'm not sure if my friends want to have a chance to look at it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I've marked it with letters and there's bars next to it, but there's nothing written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would please open it on the page you're looking at now. Yes, I can't see from here whether that's the page -- but I take it it's the page starting with "povratak, veliki nacionelni interes" --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: If my friends want to flip through it, they're marked with tabs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, they apparently have no problems with you, Mr. Carrier, so be happy.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Well, at least with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least with this, yes. No, but I thought you open it on the page the witness has to look at, so that he knows -- that he doesn't have to find his way through it at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Because they're tabbed and they're lettered, I can just say: Go to tab A on the bottom --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, if you could try to find tab B, and you'll see that tab B, there's a mark at the bottom and then it goes on to the next page. I'll continue this broken-up quote now. "We ought to define a number of stimulating measures which would motivate people to go and live in the areas where living is not so easy, or we should offer these people some other opportunities not available to people in other parts of Croatia. So the decree has a positive approach which enables the creation of opportunities which is meant to help these people who suffered a lot, et cetera ..." And, Mr. Pejkovic, if you could turn to part D, which is on page 15 in the English and it should be 15 of the B/C/S as well. And at the bottom - I'm sorry I don't have that in front of me anymore - but at the bottom of the English it says, this is Mr. Radic continuing to talk about this decree: "I would like to draw the attention to another important decree or an important decision or an important category of this decree which is directed to settling the deserted areas of Croatia ..." And on to the next page in English: "... yet I am speaking at the closed session of government. The Croats who have been expelled from Bosnia and Herzegovina - the part of Bosnia and Herzegovina under the Serbian occupation, those expelled from Vojvodina, inner Serbia, Kosovo, and other areas, therefore those who simply come from the part where the Serbian rifle in that area we are settling now in a sense of this decree - Vrginmost, Vojnic, Lapac, et cetera, we give them all the rights that returnees in Croatia have, therefore that particular category, not all the refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina, but only those which is in our national interest to settle, so those whom we have given homes, houses, space, we want to put them to survive in that area. Therefore, they are not returnees but they get all the rights as returnees in that area." And finally if you just go to part E which is on page 17 in the English and it should be page 45 in the B/C/S, but you'll see the tab. Mr. Radic says: "We have defined population areas of strategic interest to the Croats and said that the soft under-belly of Croatia, Vojnic, and Vrginmost are more important than any spot in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Therefore, that the first priority of the Croatian people's survival and populating is the Croatian soft under-belly and that is why we have agreed, mindful of all this, to move a portion of expelled persons from Banja Luka to Glamoc despite heavy pressure, et cetera. But the first priority of the overall national entity is currently to accommodate where Croatia is thinnest. And until yesterday it was thinnest, like I said, we cannot discuss this in open session, but it was thinnest in the area south of Karlovac and up to the Slovenian border, where there was just 14 kilometres of ethnically pure Croatian territory. And that is why we have accepted and agreed, as I said, to go for populating such areas of great strategic importance, even to the detriment of the overall number of Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina." And then he goes on about some data. Now, Mr. Pejkovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the question and to the method. I think it's not fair to the witness to read him from a very large document certain parts only in a situation that witness from the very beginning stressed that he was not present at that meeting and that he was not having an access to that minutes. So combining couple of parts of that large document, putting it in front of the witness, and asking him to comment that, I think it's not fair to the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there anything you would like to bring to his attention in relation to this, Mr. Mikulicic, which would complete the picture? Because the witness explained to us Monday what the basis and what the -- what the intentions with this decree were. Now, Mr. Carrier puts to him parts of a document in which the interlocutors say that this is not to be discussed openly but only in this context. If there's any part of this discussion which you would say would create a balance which you would like to be put to the witness as well, then please tell us so that we have an opportunity to give some more context to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all due respect, the witness said that he was familiar with the decree itself, not with the motives that were discussed in the closed session of the government. So what he can comment is the subject of the decree, which was publicly announced in the public newspapers in Croatia, where those types of laws and decrees has been published at the time. And so I think without going through all the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Mikulicic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: -- and to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the basic idea behind this document was to stimulate the return of displaced persons. The witness gave his ideas on what the basic background was. We can't now say that he hasn't seen this. Something is put to him by Mr. Carrier which may change or may not change his views on the matter, but the witness told us about the basic ideas behind it, and that is apparently what Mr. Carrier is testing and challenging. And he's entitled to do that. And if you have anything you would like to add to that -- if the witness says: Well, if they said that, I wasn't aware of that, I have no explanation for that, then it's fine. Then we have the testimony of the witness, we have the decree, we have the minutes, and then the Chamber will have to find its way through all of that. If there's anything you think the witness should be -- or if you say: Well, let the witness read over the next break pages so and so, then we'll ask him to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand. But my position was that the witness could comment only the text of the decree and in that sense what was the purpose of that decree, but not the conversation that has been put on on the closed meeting of the government. That was my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. Nevertheless, when he commented on this you didn't stop him and say: I'm not interested in backgrounds, but we see -- if the witness hasn't seen this before, it's just put to him and we do understand that he had not seen this document any earlier when he said: I'm familiar with it, I take it he was referring to the decree which also appears in this document and therefore not with the whole document. If there's any suggestion as to what context should be given to the witness, you are invited to give it. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, my objection is an 89(C) objection as to the relevance of this line of inquiry. What is being described here as far as movements within their own borders of population is perfectly legal in international humanitarian law. What's the relevance of this? So my objection under 89(C) is a request for an offer of proof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the witness testified about what the basic idea behind this document was and Mr. Carrier is fully able to test that part of the testimony. If it was relevant --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if it was relevant in chief, then it is just as relevant now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I take Your Honour's point, if it is an issue of credibility, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll see what comes out. We do not know yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On my point with regard to if there is some substantive issue here legally, I would ask for an offer of proof. If not, I would object under 89(C).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's on the record. Mr. Carrier, any wish to respond to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I think it's clear what the point is. This is about a -- a discussion about what the purpose of the decree was in addition to what Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, the point is not clear --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But what is legal and not legal, we'll first have to look at what the witness tells us. And if you say: Well, this kind of -- on face value, ethnic considerations of settling refugees in areas which were ethnically thin Croatian, if you say that is totally irrelevant to the matter, ethnic considerations for -- for decrees for which the apparent reasons discussed here could not be openly discussed -- if you say that's all irrelevant, then if that's your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or would you say that if you move from one place to another place on Croatian territory, that that is not illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's not illegal whatsoever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- for a country to say: We want to populate a particular area. This is our country. My -- what I'm concerned with under 89(C) is some inference coming from the Prosecution that moves by the Republic of Croatia to populate their own areas is somehow improper under international humanitarian law, and it is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, "their own areas," it's far more complex than you present it at this moment because it's also the way in how they were moved into the territory, their -- that's not -- the decree also talks about giving the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Serb property which was left by the Serbs. It's a rather complex picture, Mr. Kehoe, and I cannot follow you and therefore deny the objection that it is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if I may, if Your Honour can't follow me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- then let me just go to one point that was brought up by the Prosecution, which is using the term "colonise" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, we're not going to discuss that. I'm aware that the word "colonising," settling, where to settle, what areas, what territories, and whose houses you would live, how people left those houses, how easy or how difficult it was to return to those houses gives a rather complex picture and this is maybe a part of that picture, and to that extent it cannot be denied relevance on the basis of what you said. And therefore Mr. Carrier may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, my objection is on the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Also just for the record, the Prosecution's position is it does show intent in terms of the JCE and intention to put people in a place where Serbs had been living.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's precisely the point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- let's hear from this witness what he can tell us about what is put to him. I do understand, Mr. Kehoe, that your understanding of colonisation, deserted areas, et cetera, might be a different one from the way in which Mr. Carrier interprets these terms, that the context which is relevant for you might not be exactly the same context as it is for Mr. Carrier. Both parties have an opportunity to create their context, to put questions to witnesses on the basis of their understanding - right or wrong - of the situation as long as it's fairly done, and up to this moment there's no unfairness in the questioning. Please proceed, Mr. Carrier --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, just on the use of the word "colonisation," if I would ask for precision on the use --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, there comes a point where there is a ruling and then that is the starting point for further debate, but is if you have any further thing you would like to submit, then you can do that at a later stage. At this moment, Mr. Carrier is allowed to proceed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, did you know or were you ever aware of the fact that the Croatian government was discussing means, which included this decree apparently, to motivate Croats to colonise or settle the territories that had been liberated for strategic purposes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I object to the use of colonisation. Without the precision for that word under international law. I object. And it's not in the transcript as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I said colonise or settle to cover both basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if you use two words then each of these words should have been justifiable. So to say: Well, I used five words so if one of them is not correct, that's no problem because there were four others, that is not the way to proceed. Could you please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, were you aware that members of the Croatian government were discussing ways, which included this decree, to motivate Croats to settle in the liberated territories after Storm for strategic purposes?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim with full responsibility before this Tribunal that I was not familiar with the topics discussed by the Croatian government. I'm only familiar with the decree on the return of IDPs and refugees to the newly liberated territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, in paragraph 19 you state that the entire repatriation process -- project was open to both the domestic and international public. You said that press conferences were constantly being convened and that problems in the field were not covered up even though they were huge, and that the Serbs' returned to Croatia was followed by practically the entire Croatian press, together with representatives of the international community. And in paragraph 20 you say that the entire repatriation carried out through the ODPR and the Working Group was done in agreement with the international community. Mr. Pejkovic, my question is: Given this openness on the part of the Croatian government and the fact that international observers were following the return of process for Serbs, is it fair to say that internationals, diplomats, and observers on the ground, were given free access to monitor the return process and how Croatia carried out that process? Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire process was transparent and open. As for the government, the office employed 250 employees, as I've already mentioned. There were also -- there were several times more different kinds of monitors. Each individual return that took place was followed by several international or NGOs which were active in Croatia, which were active in the liberated areas of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So I take it that internationals were given free access to monitor the return process?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was fully free access without any obstacles. As I have said already, a copy of the certificate to return for each and every refugee was sent to the UNHCR. Once the OSCE came in and established itself in the newly liberated territory, we provided information to them as well on each individual return.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we please have Exhibit D1829 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, what's coming up on the screen is a document that Mr. Mikulicic reviewed with you during your testimony. There's no B/C/S version of the document, so I'll have to read you a portion of it, which is on page 1 in the English. It was referred to by His Honour Judge Orie at the time you were shown it. The fourth paragraph down, this is a statement by the President of the Security Council. "'The Security Council" -- sorry, just to be clear it's dated the 2nd of July, 1998. "'The Security Council expresses its grave concern that a large number of Serb residents and displaced persons have emigrated from the Republic of Croatia since ... 1996, mainly because of continued security incidents, ethnically related intimidation, a dire economic situation, bureaucratic hurdles, discriminatory legislation, and a stalled return programme. A continuation of this trend could have a seriously negative effect on the restoration of the multi-ethnic society in the Republic of Croatia.'" And my question, Mr. Pejkovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: My question for you, Mr. Pejkovic, is: Given your testimony that internationals were basically given free access to monitor the return of Serbs, are you able to offer any explanation for why members of the international community were reporting that the Croatian government was purposely erecting legal and bureaucratic impediments to the return of Croatian Serbs after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document itself shows that there were representatives of the international community who were present in the field; they followed the process of return and pointed out certain difficulties in terms of degrees of discrimination, if there was any. They also pointed out bureaucratic hurdles which existed in Croatia. It is still an ongoing problem of the bureaucratic system in Croatia. It is inefficient, it functions poorly, and needs to be changed. However, if one takes it out of the context, one would think that the bureaucratic treated only the Serb refugees that way; it did not. It was quite uniform in its behaviour. It applied to everyone simply because that system is not efficient and works poorly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, you were appointed by President Tudjman on 9 October 1997 to the national committee for the implementation of the programme for establishment of trust, rapid return, and normalisation of life in the war-affected areas of Croatia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I was appointed a member of that commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Pejkovic, on that 12-person committee, one of the other members was Professor Pupovac - isn't that right - he was a member of the house of representatives of the Croatian parliament?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he still is an MP.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And are you familiar with a woman named Jelka Glumicic She was a founder of the Karlovac human rights committee, and she was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize in 2005. Do you know who she is?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know her personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, are you also aware that you were -- are specifically named in the press by both Professor Pupovac and Ms. Glumicic as one of the people involved in the process of return that in fact impeded the return of Serbs to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I read such press reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And in those press reports, they were actually calling for your removal from the ODPR, and you were named as basically one of the old guard and the right-hand man of Jure Radic; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When such requests appeared, Mr. Pupovac and his party were members of the governing coalition that was in power at the time. Ms. Glumicic, as a Nobel prize candidate, did not receive an important position in the government; therefore, I became the target of her anger as the head of the department for refugees and displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier -- yes, please finish your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, in Croatia, we had a coalition government, including many Serbian MPs in senior positions. They basically assumed power in certain sectors of the executive branch in the Republic of Croatia. In 2005, that is to say after almost two years of the coalition government being in place, submitted my resignation for personal reasons. I abandoned the position I had held, and although I worked through the period of time in which three different governments were in power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, I'm looking at the clock. We inspired you with -- said that the Chamber was confident that you would finish in 45 minutes. There was some disturbed examination, but would you please now come to conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. I just -- I have one more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Just in light of these articles and what you said before, Mr. Pejkovic, about how the Croatian bureaucracy was -- just generally was a problem, can you explain how these two people, at least with respect to Mr. Pupovac, was part of that bureaucracy? Wasn't it saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps we should have some preciseness, Your Honour. When was Croatian bureaucracy a problem? We're dealing with a lot of material - if I go back to paragraph 12 of this indictment - that I personally fail to reconcile with the issues in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first see what exactly the question is to start. The question again, Mr. Carrier, and phrase it in such a way that we do not end up in generalities rather than in a precise, focused question, which would be your last question anyhow. So take your chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Pupovac -- sorry, Mr. Pejkovic, given what these people are saying and specifically in terms of what you said before about the bureaucracy, the Croatian bureaucracy generally being an issue, treating everyone, regardless, basically -- your point was -- regardless of ethnicity, the same, can you explain how someone like Mr. Pupovac who was part of the bureaucracy was specifically naming you as a problem?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you answer the question, one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've put your last question to the witness. The witness is not required to answer that question because you didn't follow the guidance given by the Chamber. So therefore this concludes your cross-examination, Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Pejkovic. Concerning the cross-examination led by my learned friend Mr. Prosecutor, I wanted to ask you a number of questions to clarify certain matters. Let us start with the -- yesterday's transcript. For reference, it is page 79, line 24. You were discussing the return programme with the Prosecutor. He told you that there was certain obstacles at the time. I would like to discuss those obstacles with you as they existed in the period before the programme took place and afterwards. You mentioned that these obstacles were objective in nature. Can you tell us which were those objective obstacles which impeded an unhindered return of refugees to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Sorry, can I have a reference for the -- what he's putting to the witness about objective obstacles?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 79, I think -- is that what you gave us, Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I did, Your Honour. "Q. And, Mr. Pejkovic, would it be fair to say that the purpose of this programme demonstrates that at least up until June 1998, almost three years after Operation Storm, there were obstacles in place for the return of Serbs then they had been put in place or there were at least sufficient government support for the return of these people?" And the answer was: "A. There were certainly some obstacles." And what I was interesting is just to point out what were the obstacles.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Speaking of the obstacles that existed, I provided a simple answer without any further explications. There were houses to which returnees were supposed to go back. Many of them were damaged or destroyed. In a certain number of such houses, other people lived at the time. Some areas were still mined, other areas lacked any infrastructure in terms of utilities. And certain settlements were inaccessible because there were no roads or bridges because those had been destroyed. All those were objective obstacles for people to return and live there in normal conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, in this category of obstacles, would you also include the issue of diplomatic and consular relations with the FRY?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, one of the obstacles in any case was the absence of diplomatic relations or the fact that there were no diplomatic missions of Croatia in the territory of Serbia and Montenegro. An additional obstacle which we have been discussing during my testimony was that the Serbs, once they left the area liberated in Operation Storm, took away registry books with data on citizenships, dates of birth, deaths, land registers, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, what about the required financial resources in order to finance such a return operation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Well, two objections: One, it's leading; and secondly, it didn't arise during cross-examination. The whole -- the witness's whole statement is about this thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mikulicic, the passage you're referring to in examination-in-chief was about --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Obstacles --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- no, legal and bureaucratic obstacles. That was what the question was about. And the witness said also that they existed up till the end of the programme. So I can't imagine that houses certainly were not destroyed anymore once the programme was put in place. So you are expanding on what was asked at the time. And I take it that there would not be that much dispute that in the situations at the time financial considerations may have been important. I mean, if there's a lot of destruction, and if there's not a lot of production, you'll get into financial problems, I would say, anyhow. Now, before we go into the whole of the budget and all the details of that, which was certainly not touched upon by Mr. Carrier, I would like to give, as guidance, that you should go back to what was discussed, what was asked by Mr. Carrier, and that was legal and bureaucratic obstacles, and that was what the answers were about. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pejkovic, you worked for the office for a number of years as of the moment of its foundation until the moment you resigned. Was there an institution that the ODPR could have relied on in terms of previous experience in order to do its work? And I mean in particular methods of work, methods of data collection, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were pioneers in that field. We are thankful to the various UN agencies which assisted; however, the entire IDP and refugee situation we had was something new to Europe. It was quite different from other refugee crisis in the various parts of the world, and, as such, needed different monitoring. We kept going back to the statistics during my testimony. When we were creating the database, we were actually doing the encountering, rather than data processing, because we needed to identify each and every person. Of course, it required time and equipment as well as financial resources to do that. Thanks mainly to the UNHCR, after only one or two years we were quite well equipped, we established sound procedures; and basically the UNHCR began using our know-how to supply the neighbouring countries with similar knowledge so that they would be able to rely on our system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, what about the legal basis for the existence of the office and the work it undertook during that period of time, which regulation existed detailing the work of the office, and did that regulation exist prior to the office being established, and was it being kept up-to-date?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no regulation in existence. It was -- the office was created by a governmental decree of the 20th of December, 199 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the year. We apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any case, no one had the knowledge or possibility to deal with such an en masse population fluctuations which took place involving refugees and displaced persons. It was partly covered by the foreign ministry, but only to the extent of those who sought asylum, if there were any such applications at the time in Croatia. When speaking of the regulation as it is now, in Croatia it would be completely impossible for one to attain any status under this programme. It can only be attained via an asylum law and provisions. Should there be another crisis tomorrow, we would have to rely on that. What I'm trying to say that there were no previous institutions covering that topic. Everything was done ad hoc, including the legislative framework. It was lagging behind. The legislators simply followed the developments in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us 20th of December of what year exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 25th of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction:

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 21st of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On several occasions, you mentioned the agreement on normalisation, which is D412, dated August 1996, as one of the key moments in the resolution of this issue. What is the importance of cooperation of all the states of the former Yugoslavia that were affected by the refugee crisis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Number one, I don't know that it's actually D412; and number two, I object because this is something that Mr. Mikulicic already went through in his examination-in-chief with this witness about the normalisation, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would say that I touched this topic but in a different sense. Now what I'm interested in was provoked by the cross-examination of my learned colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On what subject exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On the subject of cooperation, whether states on a territory of former Yugoslavia, what was the importance of that cooperation because of the huge movement of population through that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One or two questions fine, but it's really not something that could be said to have been triggered by the cross-examination. So if you would keep it short.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pejkovic, I have a short and direct question for you, and I would kindly ask for a like answer. What is the importance of cooperation with all those countries which were affected by the refugee and IDP problem in order to resolve this issue? To be more precise, can that issue be resolved by initiative of only one state in that territory?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cooperation is essential because as Croatia accepted to do in this case unilaterally, a state can organise the process of return and reconstruction. However, this has negative consequences in the field because those people who had to go the other way, to the other states, unless this is enabled for them to do, become opposed to their government's effort. And the government needs to invest additional time and resources to appease the dissatisfied population. I'm trying to say that the return should take place both ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: A UN document was quoted this morning mentioning the so-called catch-22. The context was that it was impossible for those who were outside Croatia to enter Croatia without valid documents. As you said yesterday, Mr. Pejkovic, there was a go-and-see programme in place. Can you tell us what the relationship of that programme is to the catch-22 situation as referred to in the UN document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, before we receive an answer to this question, I would like to have clear time context to be given. So this go-and-see visits, when was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that was in 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mikulicic, isn't it true that the catch-22 situation was before 1998, it was before a consulate was established in Belgrade. So, therefore, I think that the go-and-see visit could not explain what happened two years before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will rephrase, then, questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: -- on other topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pejkovic, since, in the United Nations document, the difficulties in obtaining Croatian documents is mentioned, because there weren't any places in the FRY where they could be obtained, you mentioned the role of the UNHCR in this whole process. Could you be so kind as to tell us what the UNHCR role was just briefly and what possibilities existed.

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UNHCR was and remains the leading United Nations agency for the assistance in the return of refugees and the care and welfare of refugees. The UNHCR also provided, either independently or through a network of its partners of non-government organisations, lots of possibilities, and they were active in all the states that emerged after the disintegration of Yugoslavia, which helped applicants to obtain the documents they needed. And if a person could not physically obtain the documents themselves on the territory of Serbia, then certainly some non-governmental organisation would do this in some other office where it was registered in Croatia, because there was no obstacle in that sense. However, the fact remains that until diplomatic offices were opened and consulates were opened in Serbia and Montenegro, this could not be obtained on that territory. But to put things in context, at that time in 1997, before the return programme was implemented, we were developing a process of return from Eastern Slavonia. And based on the report by Mr. Klein, 150.000 passports were issued and ID cards as well, citizenship certificates, et cetera, and we know that there were only 78.000 Serbs living there, which means that the difference between those two figures were Serb refugees who came in from Serbia to the Croatian Danubian region and obtained their documents there. And that is why we have a significant, spontaneous, non-registered return over all those years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm not sure if we're taking a break, but I just wanted to alert the Chamber to an oversight on my part. I meant to tender 65 ter 5003. There was some back and forth, and it was -- it -- part of it was D412, I think, but it's -- if I could tender that now. And I apologise, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps you better wait until I would have announced the break and then -- but, Mr. Mikulicic, we have now heard a very long answer. We now know what, in general, the role of the UNHCR is, something which I couldn't say comes as new and very important information. Then we know that some NGOs would go to some offices to settle a matter. And now we see what happened in the Croatian Danubian region, all of it not of great assistance to the Chamber. Could you please try to focus your answer. And if the witness goes in different directions, then to take care that you guide him into the right direction again. And could you tell us how much time you would still need approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Five minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, then you even stay well within -- if it would be five minutes, then I think it would be wiser to have the break after those five minutes. Again, you asked for more, and you are entitled to more, but if you think you can finish in minutes, that's, of course, appreciated. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pejkovic, you told us that your office had a large database on displaced persons and refugees on the territory in which you were active. Do you happen to know whether, in similar fashion to your organisation on the territory of Yugoslavia, there was a similar office or institution, a kindred one?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were similar offices on the territory of Serbia, Montenegro, and Bosnia-Herzegovina, but they weren't organised, and they didn't have the kind of database that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On the territory of Croatia, was some other institution, domicile institution or international one, active in collecting a database, just like your organisation?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was no other, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, you said that you cooperated closely with the UNHCR, that is to say your office did, and I think you even said that at one point the UNHCR made use of your database. Now, from the UNHCR some other institution or organisation, did you ever receive complaints, criticisms, of your methodology or the results that your office had and informed others the figures you arrived at?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we never received any criticisms or complaints.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now, your office compiled two reports, one in 1995 and the other in 2000, which are exhibits in this trial, and we've been through them. Now, did you ever receive any complaints or criticisms to those reports in the sense that the facts were not correct or the methodology used was not valid or any other complaints or criticisms of that nature?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never, we were never criticised, either by the domestic or foreign institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers, Mr. Pejkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll first have a break. We'll resume at five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has the re-examination by Mr. Mikulicic triggered any need for cross by any of the other Defence teams?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I see the same position from Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, Judge Gwaunza has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Yes, I have one question, and it relates to something that is in your statement, paragraph 10. You mentioned in that paragraph that - and I'm quoting: "In principle, the potential returnees to the liberated areas fell into three categories ..." And I'm interested in the middle category where you say: "Humanitarian cases, persons whose return was requested by members of their families in the RH or particularly sensitive cases." And my question is: Could you give us an example of what you are referring to here as particularly sensitive cases?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, those are cases where the remaining members of the family were old and infirm and who had asked for the return of their family members so that they could take care of them in their old age. Then we have other cases where people were sick. We had people suffering from mental diseases, for example, children who were left without their parents. So all those were the difficult particular cases to which we gave priority to enable the family members to join up as soon as possible and thus be able to care for each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Kinis has also one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, I wanted to ask you two questions. The first is: During examination, there was touched on a question regarding Croatians obstacles for crossing borders, and even in situations were persons were obtained their certificates, they were not allowed to cross borders. My question is: Were you aware of any situations when displaced -- where persons, in order to justify return process, had been used false documents, passports, certificates issued by your organisation or Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, certainly there were some such cases, whereby Croatian documents were forged, whether they be passports or ID cards or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Was such situations in mass scale, or it was just a few or occasional and did not create for you big problems?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour - and this was shown to be the case - that, among the displaced persons and refugees, there wasn't too much of that. It was more within the criminal section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: And the next question is -- my question is related to your statement, paragraph 20, and I will quote just one portion from this statement: "However, the question of Serbs' return to the RH has been used as a constant political pressure on the Republic of Croatia, often without objective assessment of many problems ..." What are you referring to regarding this lack of objective assessments, and how do you respond in such situations?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I mean first of all that what was asked for was that everybody return in the space of one day practically, and all the criticisms that were made were directed in that direction, that is to say, not to allow the speedy en masse return because that wasn't possible. It wasn't possible to organise this because of the problems that existed that we've raised earlier during this testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much for those answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you as well. Could we have a look at your statement. Do you have a hard copy of your statement with you? If not, could it be provided to the witness. May I take you to paragraph 7 to start with. You're giving a picture there of Serbs leaving during Operations Flash and Storm, and you give the numbers. Now, in paragraph 8 the first line reads: "Immediately after Operation Storm, and after they had left Croatia, a smaller number of Serbs who were accommodated in Serbia started requesting to return to Croatia." Would that include or would that not include Serbs who had left during Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, if they were located in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we have to understand immediately after Operation Storm rather as a reference to the time than as to persons who had fled during Operation Storm, because it would cover also those in Serbia who had fled during Operation Flash. Now, paragraph 9 refers to the period May 1995 to May 1996, requests from 30.000 persons who had left the Republic of Croatia. May I take it that it also covers those who had left during Operation Flash and Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see you're nodding "yes." That's now on the record. Now I take you to paragraph 11 which reads that: "Until May 1996, the ODPR resolved 5.895 repatriation requests ... who had left ... during Flash and Storm." It then continues: "Also, the border police were issued recommendations, so-called approval for the repatriation and entry into the Croatian republic of 8.022 persons on the basis of family reunification on humanitarian grounds." Now, are the 5.895 included in the 8.022? Because the one is dealing with requests and the other apparently is giving instructions to the border police. It's not entirely clear to me whether, if a repatriation request was resolved, whether that would resolve also in an instruction to the border police whom to allow entry into the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are two figures which are independent of each other, because in the Croatian text it says also the police were issued so-called approval for -- so we have that connective word "also." And -- so there should be a plus sign between the two figures, one plus the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So all together, therefore, it was approved that some almost 14.000 persons could return. Now, I'll take you to paragraph 12 where it says that 7.000 persons returned, which means that only 50 per cent would have used their permission to return to Croatia. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, close to 6.000 had asked for repatriation, and is there any explanation as to why they first asked to return to Croatia and then do not use the opportunity to do so?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the whole process of return, repatriation, took place over a long period of time. So these facts and figures were true at a certain date. So on the one hand we had how many approvals were issued for repatriation, that figure, and then how many were consumed, that is to say, taken up on and used. The figure shows that about 50 per cent were used, which does not mean that over the next period of time the rest didn't use the approvals they were given. But there was always a certain time gap and lagging behind between the time that the papers were issued and obtained, the approval for repatriation given, to the actual physical return of the persons in question and recording that same repatriation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now I see that there will be some time gap, but if 8.000 people are seeking family reunification and got permission to return by May 1996, only 450 - or to be more precise - 447 would have used that, that is approximately 5 per cent of those -- and, I take it, were desperately seeking to be reunited with their families. Now, I can see that if you issue permission that it may take one month or two months before you're ready to travel to your family and to return or perhaps three months, but only 5 per cent of the border laissez-passer people comes as -- well, as a surprise. And looking at this percentage, would this still be fully explained by some time gap?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, 5.192 persons did return on the basis of the approval given --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean that the 5.000 -- I have to relate the 8.000 to the 5.192. Yes.
