Now -- but then the next question is when 5.895 repatriation requests were resolved - and I think your testimony was that they, of course, got permission - then it comes -- but that's a different surprise, it comes as a surprise that less than 2.000 would have used that. Where I take it that if you file a request and if it has been resolved, that you receive notice of the decision taken. That's a very small number relatively, far less than the third, that would use that. Any explanation for that apart from -- I mean, I can imagine that if on day X you have granted 10.000 requests, that on that same day perhaps only 7- or 8.000 have used the permission given to them prior to that date and that some are still to follow. But these numbers are relatively low in relation to what was apparently granted to those who had specifically requested to be repatriated.

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're talking about the period of 1995 to 1996, and that was the time when we still did not have an agreement on the normalisation of relations with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. There was still strong propaganda going on towards the Serbs, potential returnees, telling them not to go back because Croatia, they said, would not guarantee their return or their safety and security or their property or their other rights. Now, given this kind of propaganda from the Serb side and in fact in all Croatian environments they were not taken back with any joy, we could not expect that the 100 per cent who had requested -- requested approval and received approval would take them up on that and consume that right, that is to say, go back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could a reason have been that houses of Serbs were given to Croats and that they were hesitant to go back and find their houses being given to Croatian citizens?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, what this was about was to reunite, for humanitarian purposes, families and family members, which means that the bulk of the family was in Croatia already in their own homes, and that, for these first, cases there were no obstacles of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. One last question: The numbers in paragraph 12 of your statement, that is the return of 7.000 persons, that covers all areas of Croatia where Serbs returned, that is, not just the Sector South, but also other parts from where Serbs had fled. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Our reports always refer to all areas covered in Croatia that were free at the time and where the Government of Croatia had control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you said it was due to Serb propaganda to say that it was not safe to go back to Croatia. Was there ever any experience in any of the areas, whether Sector South or elsewhere, that, upon return, that what you said was propaganda turned out to have some level of realism, that is, that people were harassed or were not welcome, very frankly?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in my testimony I did say that those returnees were not always welcome everywhere they went. There were incidents, and they did take place; however, not to the extent at which one could say that this was a general rule that would be valid across Croatia. There were areas to which it was more difficult to organise the process of return; then there were areas in which it was easier. It all depended on the local authorities on the ground and their position towards the returnees, that is to say, to the implementation of the national programme of establishing trust --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. We were talking about the percentage which were allowed to return but did not return. So we're talking about May 1996, not what happened after 1998. So could you please focus your answer on that early period. Was it the same, that there were incidents in these early periods as well; were they stronger, these incidents; were they more frequent; were they not?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, immediately after the process of return began, there were many more verbal incidents. There was a number of physical incidents involved as well. But, gradually, the number of incidents decreased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you'd say this was what was reported, although the reports exaggerated and that's where propaganda comes into play. Thank you for those answers. Mr. Carrier, do you have any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have the questions of the Bench triggered any --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just briefly, Mr. President, if I could ask two minor questions based on the questions that Your Honour asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm sure Your Honour hasn't forgotten, but I raised the issue of 5003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I have not forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Kehoe:

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions, sir, concerning -- just a follow-up on some questions asked by the President concerning a discrepancy between documents that were requested by Serbs in Serbia and the actual numbers of people that came in. And, again, we're talking about the numbers that you were discussing with the President in paragraphs 11 and 12. Now, concerning the desirability of getting Croatian documents, passports, et cetera, at this time in 1996, someone with a Croatian passport and travel documents was permitted to travel to European Union countries based on those documents, whereas somebody that had a passport only from the FRY, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, needed a visa to travel to European Union countries, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: It is leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is leading. It is cross --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I apologise, it just -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know -- well, I wouldn't call my questions to be examination-in-chief, but at least Mr. Kehoe did not call this witness, and he's - as far as I'm aware of - not prevented from leading, apart from whether the leading would do any harm in relation to this question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I think the witness responded "yes" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: My next topic has to go with the comments that you made, sir, concerning propaganda by the Serbs during 1995 and 1996, which you noted prevented their return or tried to tell people not to return. And if I could turn to D1610. As you note from this article, this is an article that's dated 7 March 1996, and it deals with a multitude of issues concerning the return of Serbs to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But if we could go to the bottom of page 2, I know that's page 2 in the English, if we could scroll down to the bottom of page 2 and I am referring -- yes. It's the comments beginning with Dr. Babic, and it is in the bottom of page 2 in the B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And if you could take a look at this, sir, and, if I may, it reads that: "Dr. Milan Babic who claims that he has not met Borislav Mikelic since the exodus of the Serbs from Krajina and that he therefore knew nothing about the intentions of the committee but what he was told by third parties says the following: "I am not in favour of individual solutions of the problem of returns, because it would mean" -- if we can turn the page in English and stay on the page in B/C/S -- "'Croatisation' of the Serb returnees which would jeopardise collective rights of the refugees and blur the problem of the Serb people in exile. I am in favour of collective return, collective security, and collective rights of the Serbs which implies a resolution of their political status." And it goes on through some additional discussions. And if I can just read the next part: "Because the Serbs from Krajina," Dr. Babic continues, "have the political right to the territory of Krajina." Now, that is an item that's in the record, sir, at this point, but is this the type of media and/or propaganda that you were thinking about when you referred to some of the difficulties being presented by the Serb authorities in trying to convince people not to come back?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, those who led the Serbian people out of Croatia founded their government in exile. They also controlled certain organisations and associations of those Serbs, which campaigned among the refugee Serbs to put forth political requests which would have -- first have to be implemented before a collective return of Serbs to Croatia could take place. In such a way, they practically tried to talk the refugee Serbs into not going back, because they knew that if they wanted to go back, they would have to become Croatian citizens who recognise the Croatian authority and its institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Is there any objection against admission of 65 ter 5003?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That is the document that Mr. Misetic raised a question concerning the translation. If we could MFI it at this point and then have a review of that, we would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you would say if there is an accurate translation, there are no other objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit P2678, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And keeps that status. Mr. Carrier, when do you think that you could report to the Chamber that the translation has been verified? [Prosecution counsel confer].

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: By the end of next week if that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the end of next week. I don't think there's any more urgent -- the most important is that we have an accurate record. This then concludes your testimony, Mr. Pejkovic. You've been here with us for a couple of days. You've answered all the questions put to you by the parties, by the Bench. I would like to thank you for coming, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could I only ask you to be allowed, at the close of my testimony, to greet the generals?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, my usual answer to that is - and that's for you today as well - that the mere fact that you expressed your wish to greet them has reached them, and they've heard that. And that could be considered as a greeting. But usually there's no room for a witness to greet accused persons. But it's on the record, they've understood it, they've heard it. So to that extent, your wish is communicated to them. Could you please follow the Usher and ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I wonder whether this is an appropriate moment to decide upon D1825 and D1826 MFI, which is a statement and supplemental statement of the witness Pejkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's first ask Mr. Carrier whether he wants to add anything to the objections that were filed, whether you still adhere to them or whether you withdraw or withdraw some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: The objections still stand I think, given the testimony as well. You will recall his reference to him putting algorithms, et cetera, in terms of producing numbers. Again, it's the same objection. It's difficult to test that and know whether they're accurate or how they've been produced so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Carrier. Any of the other parties who would like to add anything to a discussion on admission?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President. On this score, I don't see the difference in this issue of a gentleman coming in and giving a list of numbers that he took from a system, how that's any different from the system that the Prosecution put forth in the documents concerning UNMO burning of villages. In fact, it would -- I submit to the Chamber that the document -- the numbers that were offered by this witness were significantly more accurate. And I can use as an example some of the more recent comments that have been raised, and that has to do with this 200.000 number that Mr. Carrier used from the UN document. Those types of numbers have been used routinely in this case, and we simply have been unable to get behind them. And I submit to the Chamber that when we have been able to get behind them, we have called those numbers into serious question. This gentleman's testimony was simply that: Conveying to the Chamber a list of numbers and statistics that they have compiled over a significant period of time from 1991 through over -- well past 2000. It is nothing more than that. And I think that not -- taking these numbers as they are and accepting the numbers as been presented by the OTP in their case is, I submit to the Chamber, a distinction that shouldn't be permitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as the 92 ter statement of the witness is concerned, the Chamber admits it into evidence with the exception of paragraphs 18, 19, and 21, partly due to the witness presenting opinions and partly due to the fact that matters have been covered by oral testimony and that the Chamber uses its discretion not to admit, in this respect, portions of paragraphs 18, 19, and 21. As far as the statistics are concerned, one of the objections was that it would need expert knowledge to present that kind of evidence. The Chamber noticed that the statistics are not -- first of all, that the statistics just represent what was gathered as numbers, whether correct or wrong, but the witness has given these numbers as registered. During the examination of the witness, quite a lot of attention has been paid to what the numbers do tell us, what explains certainly falling or rising numbers, or what were estimates, 120.000 against 200.000, on what they were based exactly. The factual bottom line here is that this is how the numbers were compiled. The Chamber further notes that no complex statistical analysis was made with them; there are no correlation issues; there's no -- there are no analysis made in order to establish correlations. It's rather plain information. In view of the explanations given by the witness, the Chamber considers these paragraphs. These were, I would say, the lower and the earlier paragraphs to which the Prosecution objected, that they can be among the paragraphs that are admitted into evidence. As far as the supplemental information sheet is concerned, there were no specific objections to that, Mr. Carrier, were there?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The supplemental information sheet can therefore be admitted into evidence. Mr. Registrar, could you please assign numbers to the 92 ter statement and the -- no, they have been assigned numbers already. Could you please repeat the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe the 92 ter statement was marked for identification as D1825, and the supplemental information sheet was D1826.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. D1826 is admitted into evidence. D1825 is admitted into evidence with the exceptions -- exception of paragraphs 18, 19, and 21. And the Markac Defence is instructed to upload a version of this document in which paragraphs 18, 19, and 21 are redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We'll act accordingly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. I don't think that anything remains in relation to Witness Pejkovic. Are you ready to call your next witness, Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That will be Mr. Kuzmanovic's job, so I will leave him in my place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Kuzmanovic, your next witness will be ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. It's still morning, three minutes. Mr. Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pavlovic, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration before you give evidence. May I invite you to make the solemn declaration, of which the text is now handed out to you by Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, you will first be examined by Mr. Kuzmanovic. Mr. Kuzmanovic is counsel for Mr. Markac. Please proceed, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I proceed, I just had a discussion, before this session began, with Mr. Waespi about adding two documents to our 65 ter list, they are a map which is 3D06-0603 and a report, 3D04-1011.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that the result of this discussion was that there was no objection, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave is granted to add them to your 65 ter list, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would ask the Usher, please -- Your Honour, with Your Honour's permission, we have a binder and with the witness's statement to make things a little bit easier to follow along, if he may have those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the binder be given to the witness. Mr. Pavlovic, you can consult the binder, but you cannot consult any other documents. So wait for instructions where to go in the binder, and your statement is available to you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to approach the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If you could please sit a little bit closer to the microphone. Thank you. Could you please tell us what your current occupation is.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I am retired, but I am also the manager of a security consulting and intelligence agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we please have 3D04-1854 up on the screen. The English version is 3D05-0644.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, on the screen is a witness statement that you gave to the Defence of General Markac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You have a hard copy of that in front of you as well?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, you recall, do you not, giving a statement to the Defence of Mr. Markac dated May 11th of 2009?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to the last page of the statement, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, on the last page of this statement, which is page 7, that is your signature at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And you recall being interviewed on May 11th, 2009?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to review your statement that's up here on the screen before testifying today?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that statement accurately reflect what you told the members of the Markac Defence?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time that you gave this statement, Mr. Pavlovic, did you give it to the best of your knowledge and in accordance with the truth?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: The whole statement was made according to what I can recall and is true in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If I asked you the same questions today in court that you were asked prior to signing the witness statement that you have in front of you and that's on the screen, would you provide the same answers today in court as you did to the questions that were posed to you during the course of the interview that led to the statement?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I would provide the same answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that this statement be tendered in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit Number D1830.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1830 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, in paragraph 2 of your statement you discuss your work for the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Croatia. Could you please tell the Chamber when you began your work with the Ministry of Interior and what kind of work you did.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I began working with the former republican interior secretariat in 1977 in the communications department. I worked on telecommunications and IT network. I took care of the IT network of the former republican secretariat of the interior, which today is the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia. Should I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's good for now, Mr. Pavlovic. I'll ask you to further elaborate on that with the following question: When and how did you get involved in working for the special police?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: In early 1990, I was assigned to the post of chief of the sector for special communications equipment; and as of day one of the creation of the special police, I was assistant commander of the special police for communications. Later on, I was also in charge of the entire operations equipment department.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, how long did you work with the special police? You said you had retired. Was that retiring from the special police or from the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. I was retired in 2000, and I left the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: From the year 2000 until today, could you please describe for the Chamber the nature of what your work is.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: For the first two years, I worked, although I was retired; and after that, I began working in this company I referred to which deals with business intelligence and security information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that position keep you in Croatia, or does it take you all around the world?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part, I am in Croatia. But I also attend different types of educational events, congresses, seminars, et cetera, all over Europe and North America.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, you, in working with the special police, have had a chance to work with General Markac for quite some time; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the course of planning for any operation, I was constantly with General Markac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to talk to you now in general about some of the discussion you have in your statement in paragraphs 19 through 22 relating to your function in communications. Your nickname is Antenna, is it not?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: A function of your communications role?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was given that nickname by General Markac because I always had two to three radio stations with antennas. One radio station has a prolonged antenna, and that's when General Markac gave me this nickname of Antenna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you describe, generally, without going into much detail, as much detail as you do in paragraphs 19 through 22, which the Chamber has and I'm sure has read, just give us an indication of what kind of communications set-up you were involved in before Operation Storm began for the special police.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I was responsible for the communications system as the most important component of communication between the commander of the operation and every other soldier, because the security of the soldiers themselves depended on it and their ability to report back, saying which positions they were in, whether they needed reinforcements, whether they were perhaps wounded and needed assistance generally, as well as reporting on their positions, as I said, and additional involvement, the additional involvement of either other units or the artillery and things like that. Now, for us to be able to ensure that that was possible, we had to secure the radio communication which was based on the analogue system, which meant that the enemy could listen in to such communications. And we had to devise a secure means of communication which the enemy could not tap into. So we had to use various code words in order to protect our communication, communication between the Main Staff, the commander, the axis commanders, and so on and so forth, everybody else involved in the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, before Operation Storm, where were you located, Mr. Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: We were at the headquarters set up in Seline near Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And you also had a communications in and around the Velebit; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. We had a forward command post, in fact, at Veliki Golic on Mount Velebit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just briefly describe for the Chamber what conditions were like up on Veliki Golic.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: The conditions at Veliki Golic were such -- well, I don't know if you know or don't know, there's no electricity, no water there. There was a sort of makeshift barracks, or rather, makeshift shed, in which we put up a number of radio stations, a wire communication between the headquarters in Seline and the forward command post. We had a fax device, and these were powered by generators. These generators created the necessary electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the elevation in terms of the Velebit and where the forward command post was located?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but it was over a thousand metres; I think at about 1300 metres above sea level, but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the Chamber not only during Operation Storm but subsequent to Operation Storm what effect the terrain had on communications, the nature of the terrain that the special police were operating in.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: The terrain itself was hilly, and certain areas had a dense forest. There were great indentations or gorges. It was very inaccessible and generally a difficult terrain to move around in, mostly rocky terrain, so difficult to walk around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And how would that affect the ability to communicate?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was very difficult because we had to ensure communication even when you were in a dense forest and when the forces were in a gorge. So we had to set up various devices in order to ensure that communication was -- existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Markac's command was in communication with the Main Staff of the Croatian army, both before and during Operation Storm; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: How would one communicate -- the Main Staff's located in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: How would one then communicate with the Main Staff in Zagreb? Would you have to be in the headquarters or would you -- could you be out in the field and speak with Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: You had to be in the main -- at headquarters to ensure communication, because there were fixed telephone lines using protective communication -- protected communication, and the second one was a modem link by computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, I'd like to take you now to a review of activities roughly from the end of July 1995 until the beginning of Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could please call up D543.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Pavlovic, that is tab number 13 in your green binder, if you could open it up. Mr. Pavlovic, D543 is dated July 29th of 1995 and it's an order from the Main Staff of the Croatian army to General Markac, essentially explaining what the special police's role will be in Operation Storm. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, in the explanation section of the order in the -- underneath where it's entitled "order," the four main objectives of the MUP special forces are listed; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, can a foundation be laid first between the witness's testimony and this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, you were aware, were you not, of this order and the contents of this order?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that was certainly leading. It could be asked: Have you seen the document at that time? Where were it seen? I see he's not listed as an addressee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's -- since when are you aware of this document, Mr. Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the contents of the document, I became aware of them on the 31st in Stari Grad, or rather, 30th of January [as interpreted], when Mr. Sacic informed all the commanders with the plan of action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just try to fully understand. So you didn't see the document at that time, but you were informed about the content; is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think the transcript says the 30th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It should be July then. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I must say, we gave our transcriber a very hard time today, so I'm surprised that it's only this small mistake that we notice at this moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No problems, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, the -- you were advised of what the four main responsibilities, at least initially, in Operation Storm were for the special police; correct, as listed in the order D543?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were informed with the assignment given the special police. And in this document, you can see that those assignments were the ones that we were presented with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, one of the main objectives of the four here was the communications tower at Celavac. Can you please explain the significance of that target.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Celavac was a enemy communications stronghold, from which they were able to intercept our conversations. And very often while we were at Velebit, they jammed our communication. Now, strategically speaking, it was a position which covered the entire Mount Velebit area. And that is why one of the tasks was that we should take control of that radio relay facility as soon as possible because we expected them to jam our communication from that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain the effect of neutralising that communication facility for the ARSK and the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: The RSK used these -- this feature for their own communications, and from that area they were able to cover the area of Gracac, Obrovac, having good communication and secure communication. So as far as they were concerned, that facility was very important to them. And when we were given our assignment, we were informed about the strong resistance that they could set up and that we could encounter at that elevation point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware what the effect was on the ARSK in terms of being able to communicate was after the Celavac relay station was captured; and if so, what was that effect?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: An attack on Celavac meant that their signalsmen and communicationsmen had to withdraw. And after that, they no longer had secure communication. All they could do was to communicate using the simplex system, which is highly restricted in terms of space and area. That means that they could only communicate within a range of optical sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, let's take us back to July 30th, when you were informed -- you testified you were informed about the operation and what was to take place. What kind of discussions did you have -- were instructed to you at that time about what you needed to do about what your fellow officers and soldiers needed to do in preparation?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think it was the 30th; it was the 31st of July, I believe. And all the commanders were informed of the axis of operations. Commander Sacic and myself, a few days prior to that, set up a communications system which was to be used. We devised a plan of communication for all participants in the operation, and we also compiled a plan of deployment for the mobile and fixed repeater stations in order to ensure good-quality radio communication. And at the meeting, we also informed all the commanders of a radio directory, a pager directory, and the code system, coded documents such as the conversation device and a code document for map reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What instructions, if any, were there in terms of how to treat non-combatants or others that you encountered along the axis of attack?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: With your permission, I can explain briefly how Commander Sacic informed us about the operation, the overall operation, what -- how he informed us. He told us of our axes, the directions in which we were to operate, how we were to secure our left and right flank or wing, which individuals we would come across from the Croatian army on our left wing and our right wing, where we would have meetings with them. And we were explained procedure, procedural matters, that is to say, what to do if we took enemy prisoners, what we should do if we came across civilians, and things of that kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, may I invite you to focus your answer on the question, because you've now explained to us what instructions you got, but the question was specifically as to instructions, if any, how to treat civilians. Could you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes. If we encountered civilians, those civilians had to be sent to the basic police force. They were to report to the police in order to ensure their documents and accommodation, food and water.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And with respect to treating non-combatants, what were you advised of that -- I mean -- I'm sorry, treating combatants that you came across, what were the instructions that you received?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: If we were to encounter enemy soldiers, we were told to disarm them, depending on their number; to leave sufficient people to guard over them; to call in the police, who would then take them over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, this was not -- was this the first time that you or any of the people you were with at that briefing received any instructions on how to deal with either non-combatants or combatants?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: In all the previous operations, we were always informed and acquainted with the manner in which we were to take the persons prisoner and how and whom to hand them over to. So this wasn't the first time that we heard about this, but the same thing was repeated again and again, the manner in which we were to behave, our conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this might be a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. Kuzmanovic. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, please proceed. And could you conclude five minutes before quarter to 2.00, because I'd like to raise a procedural issue. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, I wanted to ask you a question, before we go on, to your route that you took during Operation Storm about the number of people that you had working under you. Could you please tell the Chamber how many people you had working for you.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Directly under me, about 60 in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Chamber, was this an exclusively Croatian group that worked for you or were there other nationalities as well?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: In my sector and in the field, I had a mixed team. So most of them weren't Croats. I had five Serbs, one Macedonian -- or most of them were Croats, with the exception of these others, but they weren't exclusively Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, if you could look back at the order D543, the first part of the order there where it says "cut the Gospic-Gracac road between Sveti Rok and Stikada. Stikada was the location. What was in Stikada at the time?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Stikada was the base --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat which one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat what base there was in Stikada.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] UN base and the Jordanian Battalion was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That was -- could you explain to the Chamber in terms of its proximity to Gracac, Stikada.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: About 20 kilometres away, unless I'm very much mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, on the first day of Operation Storm, it's true, is it not, that you went through several towns on your way and ended up in Lovinac, Croatia, those towns being Sveti Rok and Ricice. Could you describe for the Chamber, as you went into those towns, what you observed?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: A correction: On the first day, we were in Seline. On the second day, we set off from Seline across Mali Alan then going down to Sveti Rok and then to Lovinac. In Lovinac, we waited for the Minister of the Interior, Mr. Jarnjak, to arrive; and then in the place itself which was a Croatian place before the war and which had been completely destroyed, there was just a chimney on a destroyed house, and we put up the sign "police station." And after that, we moved on towards Gracac. When we passed through Sveti Rok on through Lovinac and Ricice later on, we saw that all the houses had been destroyed. They were all Croatian villages by the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: As you were coming down from Mali Alan on the way through Gracac, could you describe the nature and extent of whether or not the area was heavily populated, sparsely populated?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: It was sparsely populated. And up to Gracac, there was no larger place, larger town or village along that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Before we get into your observations as you entered Gracac, Mr. Pavlovic, could you describe, in general, both during before and Operation Storm, whether or not the special police had any territorial or area responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No. The task of the special police was to act speedily and advance forward and to establish combat contact with the enemy, to rout the enemy, and continue its action. Now, behind us or after us, you would have the regular police force coming in which would take over the tasks that they were in charge of, that is to say, to secure the territory and to prevent crimes, to uncover the perpetrators if crimes were committed. That wasn't the task of the special police in Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, just to make things clear, as opposed to the Gospic Military District or the Split Military District, the special police didn't have a specific territory that it covered; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pavlovic, as the person in charge of communications, could you describe for me whether you or your subordinates were generally in the front to try to establish front communications along the way, along your axis?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Certain people working in communications in the mobile vehicles had repeater stations as mobile devices, and they went either behind the unit, immediately behind the unit that was launching an attack, or there were some dominant features, dominant elevations, and maintained the system to see that it was working. Very often we were very close to the lines of combat in order to ensure good communication with the special and for the special units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, before we get into Gracac, can you please describe for us any briefings that you had before Operation Storm, what information you had about the opposition you were about to face as Operation Storm was launched.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: According to the available information that we received from the Main Staff and the information that we had in the field itself, one could conclude that the enemy forces were strong, that we were facing strong enemy forces. And apart from the fact that on the 31st we held the meeting with the commanders of the special units that I mentioned, General Markac, myself, the assistant for internal control, Mr. Soljic, and two other individuals from the headquarters in Seline -- a day before the operation, we went on foot to Veliki Golic and the forward command post there so that General Markac could tell the commanders once again that there could be -- they could come across strong resistance and repeated his instructions and guide-lines as to what our conduct should be with any prisoners of war and civilians that we might come across during our operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, in your statement in paragraph 12 you talk about on: "The afternoon of 5 August 1995, a special police operation staff was established in Gracac." Now, if we look at D550 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could bring that up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And as we're waiting to get it up, Mr. Pavlovic, it's tab 17 in your book. I should have told that to you already. I'm sorry. D550 is an August 5th, 1995, order from General Cervenko. And on page 2 of that order, in section 3.5, MUP special units are ordered to seize control over Gracac. Now, you were familiar with that order, were you not?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was because that order reached the headquarters at Seline, and Mr. Markac conveyed the order to Mr. Sacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, upon your entry into Gracac on August 5th, can you describe what you observed as you entered Gracac.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: On the second day, we started from Lovinac for Gracac. Just before we entered Gracac, we came upon a house burning. I don't know who set fire to it, but, in any case, it was burning. There were some damaged houses lying ahead, although I couldn't tell whether it was due to shelling. We entered Gracac itself by passing next to the former police station, which used to be their police station while they were in Gracac. We went further to the centre and the municipal court building, where we established the new headquarters to further command the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived in Gracac, could you describe whether or not there were any abandoned vehicles or other items lying about in the town?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: In the town itself, as well as on the outskirts, I noticed several civilian vehicles. Some vehicles had their engine compartments visible because of the raised hood. I presume they were -- malfunctioned. There was some agricultural machinery such as tractors and cultivators. Later on, we concluded that some vehicles were simply left without fuel, while others did not function. We came upon such vehicles along the roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What was done with regard to those vehicles?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: In principle, pursuant to the order, all vehicles and agricultural machinery should be taken to a collection point which had been predetermined.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: We have been shown or the Chamber's been shown a picture of a special police member in a vehicle appearing to jump-start a vehicle. Are those the kinds of things that the special police would do, get into a vehicle and get it out of the way and move it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I'd like a linkage between the witness, whether, you know, he remembers this situation. That's certainly leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well linkage and leading is not exactly the same, but it's certainly is leading, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What did you observe, if anything, Mr. Pavlovic, about special police members and abandoned vehicles?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: We needed to remove some of the vehicles from the roads. Some vehicles were jump-started by certain special police members. Since we faced a shortage in our carpool, certain units made use of some of those vehicles in the area of operations. Some even wrote names of the units on the vehicle doors so as to prevent anyone shooting at them, since those vehicles no longer had registration plates. Therefore, one could not know, otherwise, who was in the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, there is an exhibit - and I won't call it up now, and I'll just refer the Trial Chamber P111 - that describes that after the special police arrived in Gracac there was freedom of movement between Gracac and Gospic. Could you please describe for the Chamber what the significance of the opening of that road meant as far as Croatia was concerned.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. Which part of the road?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The road between Gracac and Gospic.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: On the second day of operation, we liberated the axis between Gospic and Gracac. On day three, there was free travel between the two towns. There were no longer any reasons not to use the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And in terms of distance, what was the distance, roughly, between Gracac and Gospic, if you know, in kilometres?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately 60 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, after you were in Gracac --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could move to D552, which is tab 21 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, can I have from counsel a page reference in P111 where it says there was free travel between the two towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can read it for you. The third page. "UNMO team Gracac reported UNMO team enjoyed freedom of movement between Gracac and Gospic," which is in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine. Of course, it's a difference between the UNMO team having movement and the way it was described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kuzmanovic, if you would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: -- I can be even more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, was there any restriction of movement as far as you were concerned for any vehicles that you knew of between Gracac and Gospic after the special police captured Gracac?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were no restrictions. There were not even any check-points that were set up along that route by the regular-duty police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as you're aware, Mr. Pavlovic, with your work within the special police, were there ever any preventions of freedom of movement of UNMO or UN personnel as far as the special police were concerned?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was never an order to hinder the work of UNMO or UN personnel. Quite the contrary. On the second evening we - and I mean Mr. Markac, Mr. Sacic, Mr. Cvrk, and I - had a dinner with the Jordanian Battalion commander in their base.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could please pull up D552. Oh, I'm sorry, it's already up there. I didn't have it on my screen. I'm sorry about that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, do you have that in front of you, tab 21 in your book? And just let me know when you have it.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is an order dated the 6th of August, 1995, at 1000 hours. And on the second page the special police, special units of the MUP, are ordered to move on and continue on an axis toward Donji Lapac. Is that, in fact, what had happened?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And then there's another order, D322, which is tab 19, the same date, the 6th of August, 1995, at 2100 hours, which discusses essentially coordinating the attacks between the military districts of Split, Gospic, and the special units of the special police "to take control," in paragraph 1 it says, "of the entire territory and get to the state border." Mr. Pavlovic, is that what, in fact, ended up happening, that the special police ended up going to the state border?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please describe for the Chamber as you went from Gracac toward Donji Lapac what your observations were.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Before the beginning of the operation, I issued an order to the communications department employees to establish a forward command post in Bruvno which was along the axis towards Lapac and Mazin. During the night, between the 6th and the 7th, they went there and established that communication post. On the 7th, we set off in the direction of Bruvno. When Mr. Markac and Sacic concluded that we could go on even further afield and that Mazin was liberated, we went on. Therefore, we never made any use of that forward command post. On a plateau just above Mazin, we used several vehicles to establish a mobile headquarters. We used it for mutual communication and observed the advancement of special forces to Mazin, followed it on the maps. Therefore, we did it all out in the open.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Just to interrupt for a minute, it's Bruvno, B-r-u-v-n-o, on line 20 of page 80. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pavlovic, as you got to Mazin, that's -- Bruvno and Mazin, that's on the way to Donji Lapac, is it not?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Bruvno is along the road between Gracac and Plitvice. At Bruvno you turn right to eventually get to Mazin. Via Mazin, one arrives first at Gornji and then Donji Lapac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Before getting to Gornji and Donji Lapac, is there a place that you go through called Dobro Selo?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: On the Mazin plateau, we remain until noon. After that, we followed the line of fighters that were ahead of us to eventually reach Mazin and follow the asphalt road towards Lapac. We arrived in a village called Dobro Selo. It is a mountain pass just before one reaches the road between Lapac and Srb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, you had an occasion, did you not, to lose two communications personnel along that road; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but not at that time. If I may, I will explain. We were moving towards Donji Lapac. We stopped in Dobro Selo because the fighters who were ahead of us reported that there was a large column of civilians between Lapac and Martin Brod. They also presumed there was some enemy fighters in that column. At the same time, we also noticed another column from Srb to Martin Brod of civilians and enemy fighters. From that point, from that vantage point, we could see both columns. General Markac issued an order to stop, so as to have the column from Lapac pull out towards Martin Brod and the border. In the Srb column, there were also tanks and heavy weaponry. When they noticed our column, the tanks stopped and trained their guns at us. General Markac ordered that we should be still and not train our guns on them, although we were in no position to undertake any major activity anyhow. We only had armoured combat vehicles with machine-guns and a couple of mortars. Irrespective of that, we were ordered not to open fire at the enemy but to allow them to freely pull out of our range. When the civilian and enemy soldiers column from Lapac went through the intersection that we were going to, we continued our movement towards Lapac. Two of my personnel remained behind at Mazin with the task of ensuring -- securing communication. They followed us in the evening. Having reached the intersection following Dobro Selo, at the intersection to the left you go to Lapac and to the right you go to Srb, they got confused and turned towards Srb. They entered the column from Srb to Martin Brod, which was still there. According to our information, they drove with the column for a while when the enemy soldiers detected them since they were in a 4 by 4 vehicle, a Puch, which was not a vehicle the enemy had. They were then captured and taken to some Republika Srpska camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you please bring up 3D04-1011.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Before we get to this document, which is tab 25, Mr. Pavlovic, in your book, on August 7th, then, you and the special police entered Donji Lapac; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, in front of you is a letter from General Markac. It appears as though it's from the Seline headquarters dated 9, illegible, it says 1995. It does -- this letter relates to the missing members of your communications personnel; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And the letter says: "On Monday ..." it says "illegible," but we can presume it's the 7th of 1995, 7th of August?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. We sent the letter on the 9th because we simply didn't know where they were. We could not get in touch with them. We searched for them in the field where we had left them, trying to find out whether they withdrew to another location or went elsewhere. We simply could not think of a reason why they went missing. After this letter and after the third or fourth day as we were tapping in on enemy communications, we concluded that they were actually there. During a conversation, it was mentioned that a green 4-by-4 vehicle was left without fuel, and we presumed that it was our vehicle driven by the two staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what ended up happening that -- these two communications persons from your staff ever get returned?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: It was only after 30-odd days that we received the first information to the effect that they were alive and that they were in a camp -- were camped somewhere in Republika Srpska. And some two months later, with the exchange in the village of Davor, they were exchanged and sent back to the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could please -- I'd like to tender this document in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1831.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1831 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to go to your observations of Donji Lapac on the 7th, Mr. Pavlovic. Can you please explain to the Trial Chamber your observations as you went in to Donji Lapac with the special police.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: As we entered Donji Lapac, the first thing I observed was a heavy-duty vehicle, army vehicle, which had been hit by an artillery shell of ours. Most probably they used it to transport shells. But the vehicle had been completely destroyed. After that, from Gornji to Donji Lapac, I did not notice any destruction done to houses or anything of that kind. In Lapac itself, when I entered Lapac itself, two buildings were burning. And as I had been to Lapac before the war, the first thing I did was to go to the police station, which had been hit by a rocket. But only the building next door was on fire, whereas the police building had just been damaged. But the entire -- in the entire village -- well, there were no other buildings that had been set fire to -- by us or by anybody else through artillery action. Now, when I arrived in Lapac -- when we arrived in Lapac, General Markac went to the base, the UN base there, because in the evening we had been to the Jordanian Battalion, as I told you earlier on, and we had talked to the commander, and we told him on that occasion that he should tell his soldiers who were in Donji Lapac that they shouldn't move out of the area in which they were in, out of their facility. And that they should wait there until we entered Lapac. And that's why General Markac went to the base straight away, to meet their commander and tell him that, to inform him that we had entered Lapac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. What happened, then, next with General Markac, how long of a visit with -- of that -- strike that question. How long of a visit was it, and where did he go that same day?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: General Markac stayed there for a very short time, that is, in Lapac. And he returned by the same road, moving towards the state border via Boricevci, I think the place was called. Now, I remained in Donji Lapac for some time after that, and I waited for the communications men and left a number of them to set up a mobile repeater station in the primary school there. And I also ordered them to pull out the encryption devices and all the documents from the police station which might be of use to us later on when we came to analyse everything that had taken place at the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, as far as the special police units in Donji Lapac after arrival on August 7th, did those units stay in Donji Lapac, or did they go to Boricevac?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Part of the unit, the majority continued towards Boricevci; whereas in Donji Lapac, I think it was Commander Janjic who stayed on there with his unit. Part of the logistics stayed on and part of the communications stayed on too. I myself, towards afternoon - I can't remember the exact time but between 2.00 and 3.00 p.m. - I was still in the area, and that's when the shelling started from -- coming from an unknown direction -- or rather, from unknown units. And so I left Lapac immediately after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I set out towards Boricevci as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could please call up P586.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, that's tab 1 in your book, if you want to follow it there. P586, while you're looking for it --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know what the next question will be but if a foundation be established that the witness has seen the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, why don't you look at the document briefly and then we can ask you some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: With all due respect to my colleague, before Mr. Pavlovic answers any questions about it, I don't think it's necessarily -- it's necessary for the witness to have either read or known the document to be asked questions about it. I think the entire trial has been conducted in such a fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It depends on what kind of questions you're putting to him. Sometimes it needs to be established that he has seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sometimes it's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, are you aware of this document and the contents within this document?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I've never seen this document before now, but I do now about its contents because, through radio communications, I was informed with the details of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, the second paragraph of this document, Mr. Pavlovic, says -- actually, I'll start at the beginning: "On August 7th, during the liberation of Donji Lapac of the -- by the joint forces of the special police" I'm just saying that to establish that the document states that the special police arrived on August 7th. The second paragraph discusses: "... although in the town of Donji Lapac there were no greater battles. In the town centre, two houses were burning as a consequence of artillery rocket support actions." If you could look at page 2 of that document, the last paragraph. On the Croatian it can stay the way it is, on the first page. The last paragraph says: "The special police forces did not take part in fire-starting in Donji Lapac. Merely by the fact that except for the staff and logistics, all other units were at positions outside of the town and were going towards Kulen Vakuf and the units on leave were stationed and accommodated either out of town or at the edge of town." Mr. Pavlovic, does this letter by -- report by Mr. Bole of 2 October 1995 square with your recollection of what happened in Donji Lapac?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: It does tally in the part where it says that two houses were burning; however, the knowledge that I had, the awareness I had, about what was actually going on and after my departure from Lapac, in communication between Commander Janjic and Commander Sacic, which was conducted through a radio station device, on my way to Boricevac I learned what was actually going on, what was happening there after my departure from Lapac. So the event itself that followed and that is described here further, that is to say, the arrival of the 118th Regiment and the guards tanks, et cetera, was something communicated between radio communication between Janjic and Sacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: With respect to the last paragraph, from your observations, did or did not the special police take part in fire-starting in Donji Lapac?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, it didn't, absolutely not. When the artillery attack started from the direction of Udbina on Gracac, the commander -- or rather, I heard several shells and left Lapac, whereas Janjic called Sacic and informed him that an unknown military unit was targeting, using these weapons, and he was told to try and establish contact as soon as possible with that particular unit. After that, after their entry in Gracac itself, we realised that that was the Croatian army which had come in from the direction of Udbina. Now, during the conversations, I learned that it was the 118th Regiment, which had lost a commander and 15 of its soldiers along the way, command staff, and that they were left without any means of communication. So without knowing that the special police was, in fact, in Lapac, they opened fire on Lapac. And when they entered Lapac, that same 118th Regiment opened fire from infantry weapons and the other weapons they had, and Janjic was conveyed an order according to which the units of the special units who were holidaying in Lapac, who were on holiday in Lapac, should be relocated to the surrounding parts, so that in Lapac only the communications men and the logistics men, ten of them in all, remain there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we're beyond the time that you wanted to use; there's just one short question I wanted to ask relating to this answer and I'll ask for a short answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One short question would do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: These forces from the 118th, were they coming from the north of Lapac?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: They were coming from the direction of Udbina. Now, is that the north? It's difficult for me to say. But they weren't coming from the direction from which we entered Lapac. It was on the opposite side, and it could have been the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As the crow flies, I see Udbina seems to be west of Lapac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: North and west, Your Honour, roughly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we could discuss this not with you, but on maps it looks as if it is west but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: We'll deal with that tomorrow, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Pavlovic, we'll conclude for the day. We would like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this same courtroom. Since we have to deal with a procedural matter, could you please follow the Usher. But I would first like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony. That covers both testimony already given or testimony still to be given tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You can just leave the papers there. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, the issue I'd like to raise is the following one: We see your list of witnesses, and we see that sometimes some are taken off, some others are added. Could you -- we also saw that you asked for more time than you actually intend to use at this moment. This whole picture, could you give us any clue as to when the Chamber could expect approximately that you think you would conclude your Defence case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were discussing this, and it's our -- we thought we would get done by the holiday break, and unfortunately we're not going to be able to. I think it would be the first week or the first week and a half after the holiday break that we would be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you would say seven to ten days after we resume after the recess?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's when you expect, more or less, to conclude the presentation of your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, while we're on the topic, we would appreciate if Defence could give us the names of the witnesses who will testify in the week after next. We know the two witnesses for next week, and I guess we know the witnesses, the expert, just before Christmas. And if we could be given the names, that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: We will do so before the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 26th of November, at 9.00, in Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
